summary: Describes Xcast (Explicit Multi-unicast), an experimental multicast scheme that works well for very large numbers of small groups. Instead of routers keeping group state, the sender lists every destination in the packet itself. It complements traditional IP multicast, which scales well for big groups but poorly for many groups.

plainLanguage.summary: Normal multicast is like a tour guide with one big crowd. Xcast writes every guest's name on the invitation so no one needs a crowd list. It works well when there are lots of tiny groups.

questions: how does xcast differ from multicast
when should i use xcast instead of ip multicast
subtitle: Explicit multicast for large numbers of small groups

tldr.problem: Traditional IP multicast scales well for very large groups but poorly for many small groups. Creating thousands of distinct multicast groups requires per-group state in routers and address allocation infrastructure.
tldr.mechanism: Xcast (Explicit Multi-unicast) puts the list of destination addresses directly in the packet header instead of using a group address. Routers parse the list, partition destinations by next hop, and replicate the packet only when paths diverge. When only one destination remains, the packet becomes a standard unicast.
tldr.outcome: Xcast complements traditional multicast by efficiently serving applications like video conferencing and gaming with many small groups. However, it remains experimental due to packet header overhead and complexity tradeoffs.

today: RFC 5058 is an Experimental RFC that remains unobsoleted. Xcast has not seen widespread deployment, as applications have largely adapted to the traditional multicast model or used application-layer solutions. However, the concepts remain relevant for future small-group multicast scenarios.

sections.title: The Multicast Scaling Problem
sections.content:
IP multicast sends data from one source to many receivers using a single group address. This works well for large broadcast-like groups (a live video stream to millions) because the packet flows on a shared tree and the bandwidth is used efficiently.

However, traditional multicast has scaling problems for many small groups. Each group needs a multicast address allocated globally, and each router on the distribution tree must maintain state for that group. This creates overhead for applications like video conferencing, online gaming, and collaborative tools, where there might be thousands of small sessions with only a few participants each.

Xcast solves this by encoding the complete list of destinations in each packet instead of using a group address. Routers then forward the packet only toward those destinations, without needing to maintain any per-group state.
sections.plainLanguage: Regular multicast is like a radio station: you tune to one group address and listen. But when you have thousands of tiny groups, managing all those addresses gets expensive. Xcast writes the names of the people you want to reach right on the packet itself.

sections.title: How Xcast Works
sections.content:
In Xcast, the source includes a list of destination addresses in an Xcast header. When a router receives an Xcast packet, it performs a routing table lookup for each destination to find the next hop.

The router then partitions the destinations by next hop: destinations reachable through router A go together, destinations through router B go together, and so on. The router creates one copy of the packet for each next hop, modifies the destination list in each copy to include only the relevant destinations, and forwards the copies.

This process repeats at each hop until the packet reaches a branching point where all remaining destinations are on the same path, at which point the packet becomes a standard unicast packet (called X2U, or Xcast-to-Unicast). This allows routers far from the source to use normal unicast forwarding, reducing per-packet processing overhead.
sections.plainLanguage: The source says "send to Alice, Bob, and Carol." Router 1 sees that Alice is north and Bob and Carol are south, so it sends two copies. Router 2 sees that Bob and Carol go different ways, so it sends two more copies. Once there is only one destination left, the router just unicasts it normally.

sections.title: Advantages Over Traditional Multicast
sections.content:
Xcast has several key advantages. First, routers do not maintain per-session state. There are no group memberships or distribution trees, so the number of sessions a network can support is not limited by router memory or multicast routing protocol capacity. Second, no multicast address allocation is needed—the source simply lists addresses.

Third, no multicast routing protocols are required. Xcast packets automatically follow the optimal unicast paths determined by standard routing, and they immediately adapt to topology changes because they use the current routing table.

Additional advantages include easy security and accounting (the source knows exactly who the recipients are), support for heterogeneous receivers (each destination can have a different service class), and automatic reaction to unicast reroutes without waiting for multicast routing convergence.
sections.plainLanguage: Xcast does not need the router to remember who is in which group, does not need a special address for each group, and does not need special routing protocols. It is simpler and scales much better for thousands of small groups.

sections.title: Disadvantages and Constraints
sections.content:
Xcast is not a replacement for traditional multicast; it has significant tradeoffs. The main disadvantage is header overhead: each packet must carry the list of all remaining destinations, which can be large. Although the payload is still sent only once (unlike unicast n times), the header size increases with the number of destinations.

Second, router processing is more complex. Each destination in the list requires a routing table lookup and header construction for packet replication at branching points. However, this burden is offset by the fact that Xcast is designed for small groups (many small branching points rather than many recipients per tree), and routers can use optimization techniques like Premature X2U (converting to unicast before reaching the final destination) to reduce downstream processing.

Most importantly, Xcast only works with a limited number of receivers per packet. The size of the destination list is constrained by header length, making it suitable for small multicast sessions but unsuitable for large broadcast groups.
sections.plainLanguage: Each packet is bigger because it lists the destinations. Routers have to work harder at each hop. And you cannot use it for huge groups like a live broadcast. But for small groups, these tradeoffs are worth it.

sections.title: Applications and Deployment
sections.content:
Xcast is ideal for applications with many small multicast sessions: video conferencing (a few participants), online gaming (small game rooms), collaborative applications, and IP telephony. These applications also benefit from asymmetric access links (like residential broadband) where a user can receive multiple streams but cannot send them all unicast due to uplink limits.

The RFC describes several deployment strategies to transition from unicast or traditional multicast to Xcast. Tunneling allows Xcast packets to be encapsulated and sent through non-Xcast networks. Premature X2U lets routers convert Xcast to unicast early to reduce downstream complexity. Semi-permeable tunneling and using a small number of Xcast-aware routers provide intermediate deployment paths.

Complete deployment details are unresolved in the RFC, including the format of the destination list, the size of a channel identifier, and optimal ways to handle deployment across multiple domains.
sections.plainLanguage: Xcast is perfect for video calls, game servers, and chat groups. It can be deployed gradually: routers that understand it forward efficiently, and tunnels let it work over networks that do not support it yet.
